_about: Diplomacy. Every nation sits on a seven-step alignment track from Allied member to Axis member. A neutral's public opinion runs from -100 (Allies) to +100 (Axis). Each month it drifts back toward its 'home' leaning and is pushed by whoever is winning the war (momentum x bandwagon). At +/-leanAt it starts leaning (trade and treaties); at +/-joinAt it asks to join that bloc; below +/-backAt it steps back to neutrality. Players spend political capital to court neutrals; 'resist' makes some of them much harder to move. Events are history written as data: each fires once, in its window, only if its conditions still hold. In free play (open.json) the window only says when an event may first happen, an event never brings a country at peace into a war, an event marked mode 'history' is left out (the nation decides that for itself), and one marked mode 'open' happens only there. Besides annex, cede, war, spawn, opinion and join, an event can 'wake' a country that has stood aside until now (it enters at the given place on the track), and 'partition' one that ends: each share is [who takes it, the regions], the first taker on the list still in the war gets whatever of those regions the country still holds, and ground someone else already holds stays theirs. Conditions include 'war:A,B' (those two are at war), 'dormant:A' and 'anyHeld:bloc,place,place' (that bloc holds at least one of the places) and 'allHeld:bloc,place,place' (it holds them all), and 'since:event:id,n' (that event happened at least n months ago). 'reform' remakes a nation's armed forces from that month on: for each nation named, the new quality of its troops, strength of its air force, whether its command is still slow, and how many corps it can put into one attack. An event with nothing but a text is a piece of news. 'liberate' hands over ground an occupier has left: each named region he still holds with none of his troops in it passes to the first nation on the list still at war with him. 'peace' ends the war between two nations: each hands back the other's ground and takes its troops home. A partition marked 'occupied' leaves each piece of the country to whoever has troops standing in it, and the shares divide the rest.

events.text: The Soviet Union occupies the Baltic states under the secret terms of its pact with Germany.
Moscow hands Romania an ultimatum. Bessarabia and northern Bukovina pass to the Soviet Union, and Bucharest looks to Berlin for protection.
Alarmed by the fate of the Baltic states, Finland grants German troops the right of transit.
Germany and Italy settle the Hungarian claim on Romania at Vienna. Northern Transylvania goes to Hungary.
King Carol abdicates. General Antonescu takes power in Romania and invites a German military mission.
Berlin invites the states of the Danube to sign the Tripartite Pact.
German troops gather on the Danube and Sofia is pressed to choose a side.
Officers in Belgrade overthrow the regent for leaning toward the Axis, and crowds cheer the young King. Berlin now counts Yugoslavia an enemy.
Rome follows Berlin into the war in the east and promises an Italian army for the Russian front.
Japan attacks the American fleet at Pearl Harbor, and Germany and Italy declare war on the United States. America is in the war, with the greatest industry on earth behind it.
Italy is fighting beside Germany, and the United States is at war with Germany. Washington and Rome are now at war too.
After three days of fighting Admiral Darlan orders a ceasefire, and French North Africa comes over to the Allies. Germany and Italy occupy the rest of France, and Axis troops fly into Tunis.
The last Axis troops in Africa have laid down their arms. General Alexander signals London: "We are masters of the North African shores."

Two years of war have remade the Red Army. Its generals now handle tank armies and whole fronts in a single operation, and the factories beyond the Urals send them more tanks, guns and aircraft than Germany can build.

With Africa lost, a quarter of a million men gone into captivity at Tunis and the bombers over Sicily and Rome, the Italian army has no heart left for this war. Its divisions will not fight as they did.
The Fascist Grand Council has voted against Mussolini. The King has dismissed him and had him arrested, and Marshal Badoglio forms a government. "The war goes on," says Rome, and nobody believes it.

Italy has signed an armistice with the Allies and is out of the war. German troops disarm the Italian army, seize Rome and take over Italy's garrisons from the Riviera to Rhodes. Sardinia and Corsica are given up.

The Luftwaffe has lost the daylight sky. Since American fighters began escorting the bombers all the way to Berlin its fighter arm has been losing pilots it cannot replace, and what is left is kept over the Reich. The armies at the front will fight without it.

The Allied armies of 1944 are not those of 1942. The Americans have learned their trade in Tunisia, Sicily and Italy, and behind every attack now stand guns, tanks and fighter-bombers in numbers no German commander can match.

Nearly five years of war have worn the German army down. Its divisions are rebuilt with boys, older men and the half-recovered, short of lorries and fuel. They still fight with skill, but this is no longer the army of 1941.
The Gustav Line is broken. The ruins of the abbey on Monte Cassino are in Allied hands, and the road to Rome lies open.
Rome is free: the first of the Axis capitals to fall. Allied columns drive past the Colosseum through cheering crowds.

Across the Channel from Calais, Kent fills with tanks made of rubber and a phantom army under General Patton. German intelligence counts eighty Allied divisions in England where there are barely forty, and expects them at the Pas de Calais.

Paris is free. The city rose against its garrison, General Leclerc's French 2nd Armoured Division drove in to finish it, and General de Gaulle has walked down the Champs-Elysees to Notre-Dame through a million people.
Brussels is free. The Guards Armoured Division drove seventy-five miles in a day to reach it, and the crowds would not let the tanks through.
Behind the retreating German armies the French Forces of the Interior take over town after town. South of the Loire and west of the Rhone, France has freed itself.
The German garrisons left behind on the Atlantic coast of France, cut off since the summer and watched by the French Forces of the Interior, hold nothing now but their own perimeters.

Operation Market Garden has failed at the last bridge. Three airborne divisions were dropped along a single road to the Rhine at Arnhem, and the tanks sent up it to join them did not arrive in time. The war will not be over by Christmas.

Out of the fog and snow of the Eifel two panzer armies have broken through the thin American line in the Ardennes. The front bends back fifty miles toward the Meuse: the newspapers are calling it the Bulge. At Bastogne the surrounded garrison was asked to surrender and answered in one word: Nuts.
The Bulge is gone. The last German offensive in the West has cost the Reich its reserve of tanks and fuel, and the Ardennes are back in Allied hands.
Aachen has surrendered to the US First Army after three weeks of fighting from house to house: the first German city to fall. Beyond it the West Wall still holds.

The siege of Leningrad is over. After nearly nine hundred days the German guns have been driven out of range of the city, and Moscow fires a salute of 324 guns. More than half a million of its people died of hunger and cold.
Sevastopol has fallen and the Crimea is Soviet again. What is left of the German Seventeenth Army is taken off the beaches of Cape Chersonese under fire, or surrenders there.

Minsk is free, and the tanks of two Soviet fronts have met west of it. Behind them the German Fourth Army is cut off in the forests: Army Group Centre has ceased to exist. It is the greatest defeat the German army has ever suffered.
Warsaw has risen. With Soviet guns heard across the Vistula, the Polish Home Army has come out into the streets against the German garrison and holds much of the city centre.

King Michael has had Marshal Antonescu arrested and Romania has changed sides. Its army turns its guns on the Germans, the Red Army drives for Bucharest and the oilfields of Ploiesti, and the German Sixth Army, destroyed once at Stalingrad, is cut off for the second time.

The Soviet Union has declared war on Bulgaria and crossed the Danube without a shot fired. A new government in Sofia has declared war on Germany, and the Bulgarian army marches with the Red Army into Yugoslavia.

Finland is out of the war. Marshal Mannerheim, now President, has signed an armistice with Moscow: the frontier of 1940 is restored, Petsamo is given up, and the German troops in the north are to leave or be driven out.

After sixty-three days the Warsaw rising is over. The Home Army has laid down its arms, some two hundred thousand of the city's people are dead, and what is left of Warsaw is being blown up street by street. The Red Army watched from across the river.

Admiral Horthy has announced on Budapest radio that Hungary is asking for an armistice. Within hours German troops have seized the Castle and the Regent's son, and the Arrow Cross leader Szalasi is put in power. Hungary fights on to the end.
